dialogue.text: I'm Hana Sato, 29, and I work as a purchasing assistant at a wholesale flower market. I want to apply to a part-time landscape-design program because I miss doing design work, but spring ordering is the most physical and unpredictable part of my job.
You are trying to build a route back toward design while your current work is demanding more of your body and schedule. What would make the application feel concrete?
My goal is to submit a portfolio that shows how I think about real spaces, not just pretty plant combinations. I downloaded the application guide, but I haven't chosen the first site I will study.
That gives the first open task a clear shape: one site study, not an entire new identity as a designer.

sessions.summary: Hana begins planning a landscape-design application during the market’s busiest season and defines a portfolio goal centered on reasoning about real spaces rather than decoration.

dialogue.text: I'm Japanese and I live in Nagoya, Japan. When I ask for practical help, I prefer a concise factual answer before the background because too much framing makes me lose the question.
Concise answer: give yourself a short transition between market work and drawing instead of expecting an immediate switch.

I changed clothes as soon as I got home, washed my hands, and sat by the window with only one sheet of tracing paper for fifteen minutes. I sketched the alley outside without opening my course research folder, and starting with something visible made it much easier to continue for another twenty minutes.
That worked as a transition rather than a full study plan. You reduced the jump from physical work into abstract design work.

sessions.summary: Hana uses a fifteen-minute observational sketch after changing out of work clothes and finds that a visible local subject makes continuing design work easier.

dialogue.text: I'm a woman, and I have a two-year diploma in horticulture. Mori asked me to stay late twice for supplier checks. The exhausting part isn't really the extra hour; it's that I lose the only quiet daylight I had planned to photograph the courtyard I'm considering for my portfolio.
So the same hour carries a different cost because it removes a nonrepeatable observation window.
Yes. On a normal week I can move drawing around, but I can't photograph how that courtyard is used in daylight after the sun is gone.
That distinction may help you decide which overtime requests are actually incompatible with the portfolio task.

sessions.summary: Hana distinguishes ordinary overtime from losing a limited daylight observation window needed for her landscape portfolio site study.

dialogue.text: I asked Mori if one Tuesday a week could be a predictable early finish through the application season, and I offered to take the Thursday supplier reconciliation instead. Aya said the swap was fine, Mori agreed, and for the next five weeks I knew exactly which evening still had daylight for site visits.
You made the request a trade rather than a vague plea for less work, and the predictable slot directly served the application.
I was nervous asking, but once it was on the rota I stopped renegotiating the week in my head every Monday.
That reduction in weekly uncertainty is part of the result too.

sessions.summary: Hana trades one weekly duty for a predictable early Tuesday, preserving daylight site visits and reducing repeated mental renegotiation of her workweek.

dialogue.text: My parents' plant shop is across town, and they usually ask me to help during delivery weekends. The specific problem is that the trip from my apartment to their shop and then to the evening workshop takes nearly two hours, so a 'few hours helping' changes the whole class day.
The family request sounds small when described only by shop hours, but the travel makes its real footprint much larger.

Dad tends to think of the shop as ten minutes from everything because he drives. I don't own a car, and I haven't worked out whether moving closer to class would actually help with the shop route or just change which commute is bad.
That is a useful current observation without yet turning it into a moving decision.

sessions.summary: Hana identifies travel, rather than shop hours alone, as the main cost of helping her parents on class days and notes that moving could shift rather than solve the commute.

dialogue.text: Professor Ishida said my first idea was too broad because I was trying to redesign an entire riverside. I chose one small public courtyard instead and spent an hour noting where people crossed, paused, and avoided the sun. Her next feedback was specific enough that I could turn the observations into three design questions.
Narrowing the site gave the critique something concrete to attach to, which made the feedback usable rather than global.
It was the first time the portfolio felt like an investigation instead of me trying to prove I have taste.
That shift in task definition may be worth remembering when another piece starts to feel too big.

sessions.summary: Hana narrows an oversized riverside concept to one courtyard, producing observable behavior notes and three concrete design questions after more useful mentor feedback.

Twice that week I stopped at the library instead of going home first, and I finished two study sketches before the tired-at-home feeling had a chance to settle in.

Mum also asked me to cover the holiday delivery weekend. I said I'd check the workshop dates before promising anything.
Good separation: one routine has evidence behind it, while the family scheduling request is still pending.

dialogue.text: I finally met Lian with the rough sheets. She didn't care about the wobbly linework; she asked why one path curved behind the benches, and I realized I couldn't explain that choice. The critique gave me one design problem to fix instead of the vague feeling that the whole set looked amateur.
The roughness you were protecting turned out not to be the important weakness. The conversation exposed a reasoning gap instead.
That was embarrassing for about five minutes, then useful. I went home knowing what to redraw.
That sounds like a completed thread: you got the critique you had been postponing and it produced a specific next target.

sessions.summary: Hana completes the peer critique she had delayed and learns that one unexplained path choice, rather than rough drawing quality, is the specific issue to revise.

dialogue.text: Ren and I tested the route from his neighborhood to the design school after work. We took the bus I had always ignored because I assumed the transfer was awkward. It was nine minutes faster than my usual route and had a seat for most of the trip, so that neighborhood stopped looking impractical for class nights.
You tested the actual route instead of the route you had mentally pictured, and the difference was meaningful enough to change the option set.
I'm not moving because of one bus ride, but I can at least stop ruling that area out.
Exactly; this is evidence about feasibility, not a housing command.

I checked the messages. Dad's request is confirmed. Mori asked if I was available; I never said yes to him.
That correction should prevent you from treating an unanswered work request as a commitment.

dialogue.text: I spread the board on Sora's clay table while she was cleaning tools. Instead of presenting it, I just talked through where someone would enter the courtyard, where the shade falls, and why I moved the bench. Somewhere between the wet towels and boxes of glaze, I heard myself skip one corner every time; that was the part with no real reason behind it.
The casual explanation exposed the missing logic because you were following the imagined person through the space rather than defending the board.
I came home and fixed that corner first. It felt almost silly that the gap became obvious outside a formal critique.
That ordinary setting may be part of why the explanation was diagnostic rather than performative.

sessions.summary: Explaining a design informally in Sora’s studio reveals one corner Hana consistently skips, exposing a missing rationale that she can immediately revise.

I drafted the first paragraph of the statement, but I haven't decided when to tell them the program could eventually change how much I help at the shop.

dialogue.text: I decided not to move before I even know whether I'm admitted. I still have the long class commute, though. I respond better when you offer choices instead of commands, especially when the options have different costs or time tradeoffs.
Two choices, then: use the commute for light review, or treat it as recovery and protect a short study block after arrival. You do not have to force the train into one role every day.
For now I'm using the outbound train for reading and leaving the trip home alone. That split feels less like trying to monetize every minute.
You are using the direction of travel differently based on what you have energy for, which is more specific than 'study on the commute.'

sessions.summary: Hana postpones moving until admission is known and splits her existing commute into outbound light review and an intentionally unproductive trip home.

dialogue.text: Professor Ishida gave me a page of comments and I felt that old urge to redraw everything. I turned the comments into three questions—movement, shade, and maintenance—and checked the board only against those. I finished the revision that evening without changing the parts she had not actually criticized.
You translated a broad page of feedback into three review lenses and protected the work that was already functioning.
That was much faster than treating every comment as a verdict on the whole board.
It also gives you a repeatable way to handle future critique without globalizing it.

sessions.summary: Hana converts a page of mentor comments into three design questions and completes one portfolio revision without unnecessarily redrawing unaffected sections.

But Sora has sold ceramics for years; her public process is not the same task as my admissions portfolio.
That makes her confidence a poor match for judging your current requirement, even if her openness is inspiring.
I can admire it without using it as evidence that my quieter process is wrong.
That separation protects the relevance of your own portfolio evidence.

dialogue.text: I finally told Mum and Dad the application deadline and that the program would be two evenings a week if I get in. I asked whether we could plan shop help around one Sunday a month instead of assuming I'm free every weekend. They needed time to adjust, but we ended the conversation with the next two months written on the shop calendar.
You gave them concrete dates and a proposed pattern, so the conversation could move from surprise into scheduling.
Dad was quieter than I hoped, but having the dates written down stopped us from arguing about an imaginary future.
That is a real outcome even though the emotional adjustment is not finished.

sessions.summary: Hana explains the program timeline to her parents and agrees on a one-Sunday-per-month shop pattern, turning an abstract family concern into a dated schedule.

dialogue.text: Lian listened while I explained the courtyard board for three minutes. I asked her to stop me whenever I made a claim the drawing itself didn't support. She stopped me twice, I removed those two claims, and the next run was shorter without feeling emptier.
You used the drawing as evidence and cut language that was doing more work than the design could justify.
That is the first time shortening a presentation has made it feel more accurate instead of less impressive.
That accuracy criterion may be more useful than trying to sound comprehensive.

I put a blunt pencil and cheap paper on the floor beside the low table and told myself the sketch could be ugly enough to throw away. The disposable quality of the sketch seems important: it kept continuity without demanding portfolio-level work from an exhausted evening.
Exactly. Nothing from those pages is going into the application, and that was probably why I could do them.
That makes this a continuity tool, not a hidden productivity standard.
